summary: Professional seminars, training, association and online information services (real estate, travel): low capital and easy copying make entry easy and margins thin.
Life-science research tools, lab instruments, reagents and contract research: technical know-how and IP protect offerings, but installed bases and sales channels sit with large toolmakers.
Online and specialty retail plus consumer-goods marketing services: easy to start, but dependence on marketplaces and ad platforms and scale advantages of large e-retailers squeeze entrants.
Consumer apps, educational software, events and community services: near-zero entry cost and app-store dependence, with occasional network-effect winners.
Flooring, mats, floor coverings and commercial printing: mature commodity-like products sold through powerful home-improvement and contractor channels.
Electronic components, sensors, control and test instruments sold to OEMs: engineering know-how and qualification cycles favor established suppliers with OEM relationships.
Building hardware, metal and wood building products and fasteners: commoditized goods sold through big-box and distributor channels with code approvals as the main barrier.
Pet food, treats, accessories and pet care services: growing humanization-driven demand, but easy imitation and concentrated pet retailers and e-commerce limit entrant capture.
Computer hardware, phones, peripherals and accessories: intense price competition, powerful retailers and component suppliers, and scale-driven platform leaders.
Apparel accessories, leather goods and branded merchandise: trivially easy entry and copying with contract manufacturing widely available.
Online advertising, marketing agencies, directories and review sites: low entry cost but traffic depends on search and social platforms, and network effects concentrate directories.
Books, printed matter, stationery and paper products: easy entry, heavy digital substitution and strong bookseller and mass-retail channels.
Giftware, figurines, household containers and cookware: low-tech goods easily sourced and copied from contract manufacturers and sold through powerful retailers.
Trade shows, conferences, associations, ministries, restaurants and local services: fragmented, easily entered service businesses with modest returns.
Fragrances, candles and aromatherapy products: high gross margins but brand and shelf access drive success and formulations are easily imitated.
Lubricants, fuels and additives, car-care products and auto repair and aftermarket services: mature markets where brand, distribution and OEM approvals sit with incumbents.
Mixed pharmaceuticals, medical devices and therapy products: regulatory approval and payer and hospital channels dominate, so innovators often depend on incumbents.
Promotion, exhibitions, loyalty programs, lobbying and retail-related business services: relationship-driven services with low barriers and easy imitation.
Housewares, bedding, storage, furniture and portable lighting: easily copied imported goods sold through concentrated mass retailers and Amazon.
Specialty industrial and construction chemicals, admixtures and sealants: formulation know-how and plant scale matter, and customer qualification favors established producers.
Local community services such as child care, senior care, fitness, charities and workshops: fragmented, labor-intensive businesses with modest margins.
Paints, coatings, cleaning and polishing products and car-wash services: brand and retail shelf access held by large chemical and consumer-goods firms.
Medical disposables such as bandages, gloves and syringes: commodity products bought by group purchasing organizations, so low-cost scale manufacturers and distributors win.
Business, IT, outsourcing and financial information services: broad professional services where reputation and client relationships matter more than proprietary ideas.
Telecom, media software, gaming systems and digital network technology: mix of capital-heavy networks and software where scale and installed base favor leaders.
Packaged foods and beverages: products are easy to imitate and grocery chains and distributors with slotting fees control access, favoring large food companies.
Insurance agencies, benefits administration and business consulting: licensing and carrier appointments are moderate barriers, and offerings are easily copied.
Engineered vehicle, aircraft, turbine and pump components: qualification with powerful OEM buyers and manufacturing capability favor established suppliers.
Medical practices, specialty clinics, pharmacies and some devices: licensure and payer contracting are barriers, and payers and health systems hold bargaining power.
Streaming, broadcasting, social and media-sharing apps: strong network and content-scale effects concentrate the market, with content licensors and app stores holding power.
Energy services, fuel transport and storage, oil and gas and efficiency consulting: capital, permits and infrastructure access favor incumbents, though consulting niches are open.
Restaurants, cafes, brewpubs and food retail: very easy entry, intense local rivalry, easily copied concepts and high failure rates.
Banking, investment management, insurance underwriting and staffing: charters, capital, trust and customer bases held by incumbents let them absorb new products quickly.
Hand tools, knives, power-tool accessories and machine-tool parts: designs are easily copied and big-box retailers and established tool brands control distribution.
Beauty products, salon equipment, beauty retail and services: contract manufacturing eases entry, but brand building and retail placement decide winners.
Specialty retail, mail order and online marketplaces: low barriers but thin margins, with marketplace platforms and scale retailers capturing most value.
Pharmaceuticals and therapeutic devices: patents protect innovators, but FDA approval, payer access and commercial infrastructure lie with large pharma that often licenses or acquires pioneers.
Toys, games, sporting goods and exercise equipment: fad-driven, easily knocked off products sold through a few dominant retailers.

Spirits, beverages, dairy, confectionery and snacks: brands earn good margins, but distribution (including three-tier alcohol) and shelf space are controlled by large incumbents who acquire successful startups.
HVAC, air treatment, lighting and plumbing equipment and installation: efficiency regulation, certification and dealer and contractor networks favor established manufacturers.
Networked electronic systems, IT integration, sensors and power and solar systems: technical know-how protects somewhat, but integration and channel assets matter.
Skin, hair and personal care products: high margins and easy contract-manufactured entry, but marketing and retail placement decide winners and large houses acquire breakout indie brands.
Children's media, publishing, licensed characters and merchandise: hit-driven with many substitutes, and distribution and franchise IP concentrated in large media firms.
Water filtration, treatment and sanitation equipment and chemicals: certification and dealer networks are moderate barriers in a steadily growing market.
Jewelry, watches, tableware and glassware: fragmented design-driven goods that are easy to copy, with brand the main durable asset.
Plastics, rubber, composites and packaging materials: intermediate goods with resin-price exposure and price-focused industrial buyers.
Dietary supplements and vitamins: private-label manufacturing and light regulation make entry and imitation trivial, though gross margins are high.
Counseling, behavioral health, rehabilitation and wellness services: licensure is a moderate barrier, demand is growing, and payers and employers hold bargaining power.

Orthopedic implants, surgical devices and diagnostic sensors (with some musical instrument parts): patents and FDA clearance protect, but surgeon relationships and hospital contracts favor large device makers.
Engineering design, R&D and custom software development services: talent-based firms with low capital needs and sophisticated client buyers.
Construction, development, inspection and waste services: bid-based, cyclical and labor-constrained, with bonding and licensing as moderate barriers.
Mixed bicycle and wheel parts, tobacco and smoking accessories, rentals and office equipment: mostly mature products with distributor power and regulatory constraints on tobacco.
Live entertainment, venues, cultural attractions, classes and instructional media: competes with countless leisure substitutes, with venue and licensing assets as moderate barriers.
Pizza restaurants, sauces, cheeses and specialty foods: recipes are easily copied and grocery shelf access and local competition limit returns.
Apparel: extremely easy entry and instant fast-fashion copying, with department stores and marketplaces holding channel power.
Industrial, agricultural and construction machinery, parts and equipment rental and financing: engineering, dealer and service networks favor established OEMs.
Mobile apps, online communities, SaaS and ad-tech platforms: trivial entry but strong network effects make winner-take-most outcomes, often won by fast followers rather than pioneers.
Nursery plants, fertilizers, lawn and garden inputs and pest control: fragmented growers and service firms facing big-box garden channels, with registration needed for agrochemicals.
Music acts, film and TV production, video games and consumer AV gear: hit-driven superstar markets where labels, studios, platforms and retailers capture most value.
Radio and TV programming, concert promotion and event marketing: abundant media substitutes, and consolidated broadcasters and promoters control distribution and venues.
